n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sought the face of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the house of bloodshed.”

*Translator's note:* After the preceding imperfect verbal form, the subordinated imperative indicates purpose/result. S. R. Driver comments, “…the imper. is used instead of the more normal voluntative, for the purpose of expressing with somewhat greater force the intention of the previous verb” (S. R. Driver, *Notes on the Hebrew Text and the Topography of the Books of Samuel*, 350).

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* and several medieval Hebrew mss in reading לָנוּ (lanu, “to us”) rather than the MT לִי (li, “to me”). But for a contrary opinion see S. R. Driver, *Notes on the Hebrew Text and the Topography of the Books of Samuel*, 53, 350.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The exact nature of this execution is not altogether clear. The verb יָקַע (yaqaʿ) basically means “to dislocate” or “alienate.” In {{Genesis 32:26|Gen 32:26}} it is used of the dislocation of Jacob’s thigh. Figuratively it can refer to the removal of an individual from a group (e.g., Jer 6:8; {{Ezekiel 23:17|Ezek 23:17}}) or to a type of punishment the specific identity of which is uncertain (e.g., here and {{Numbers 25:4|Num 25:4}}); cf. NAB “dismember them”; NIV11 “to be killed and their bodies exposed.”

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads “at Gibeon on the mountain of the Lord” (cf. {{2 Samuel 21:9|21:9}}). The present translation follows the MT, although a number of recent English translations follow the LXX reading here (e.g., NAB, NRSV, NLT).
*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “Michal” here, but two Hebrew manuscripts read “Merab,” along with some LXX manuscripts. Cf. {{1 Samuel 18:19|1 Sam 18:19}}.

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* and several medieval Hebrew mss in reading שְׁבַעְתָּם (shevaʿtam, “the seven of them”) rather than MT שִׁבַעְתִּים (shivaʿtim, “seventy”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fell.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading בִּתְחִלַּת (bitkhillat, “in the beginning”) rather than MT תְחִלַּת (tekhillat, “beginning of”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “until water was poured on them from the sky.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the beasts of the field.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “David.” For stylistic reasons the name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son.” See also v. {{2 Samuel 20:13|13}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lords.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stolen.”

*Text-critical note:* Against the MT, this word is better read without the definite article. The MT reading is probably here the result of wrong word division, with the letter ה (he) belonging with the preceding word שָׁם (sham) as the he directive (i.e., שָׁמָּה, samah, “to there”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “had hung them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the day.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Philistines.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* Many medieval Hebrew mss have here כְּכֹל (kekhol, “according to all”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “was entreated.” The verb is an example of the so-called niphal tolerativum, with the sense that God allowed himself to be supplicated through prayer (cf. GKC 137 §51.*c*).

*Translator's note:* This name has the definite article and may be intended to refer to a group of people rather than a single individual with this name.

*Translator's note:* This is the only occurrence of this Hebrew word in the OT. Its precise meaning is therefore somewhat uncertain. As early as the LXX the word was understood to refer to a “spear,” and this seems to be the most likely possibility. Some scholars have proposed emending the text of {{2 Samuel 21:16|2 Sam 21:16}} to כוֹבַעוֹ (khovaʿo; “his helmet”), but in spite of the fact that the word “helmet” appears in {{1 Samuel 17:5|1 Sam 17:5}}, there is not much evidence for reading that word here.

*Translator's note:* Either the word “shekels” should be supplied here, or the Hebrew word מִשְׁקַל (mishqal, “weight of”) right before “bronze” is a corrupted form of the word for shekel. If the latter is the case the problem probably resulted from another occurrence of the word מִשְׁקַל just four words earlier in the verse.

*Study note:* *300 bronze shekels* would have weighed about 7.5 pounds (3.4 kg).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads simply “a new [thing],” prompting one to ask “A new *what*?” Several possibilities have been proposed to resolve the problem: perhaps a word has dropped out of the Hebrew text here; or perhaps the word “new” is the result of misreading a different, less common, word; or perhaps a word (e.g., “sword,” so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, CEV, NLT) is simply to be inferred. The translation generally follows the last possibility, while at the same time being deliberately nonspecific (“weapon”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Jaare-Oregim,” but the second word, which means “weavers,” is probably accidentally included. It appears at the end of the verse. The term is omitted in the parallel account in 1 Chr 20:5, which has simply “Jair.”

*Study note:* The Hebrew text as it stands reads, “Elhanan son of Jaare-Oregim the Bethlehemite killed Goliath the Gittite.” Who killed Goliath the Gittite? According to {{1 Samuel 17:4|1 Sam 17:4-58}} it was David who killed Goliath, but according to the MT of {{2 Samuel 21:19|2 Sam 21:19}} it was Elhanan who killed him. Many scholars believe that the two passages are hopelessly at variance with one another. Others have proposed various solutions to the difficulty, such as identifying David with Elhanan or positing the existence of two Goliaths. But in all likelihood the problem is the result of difficulties in the textual transmission of the Samuel passage. The parallel passage in 1 Chr 20:5 reads, “Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath.” Both versions are textually suspect. The Chronicles text appears to have misread “Bethlehemite” (בֵּית הַלַּחְמִי, bet hallakhmi) as the accusative sign followed by a proper name אֶת לַחְמִי (ʾet lakhmi). (See the note at 1 Chr 20:5.) The Samuel text appears to have misread the word for “brother” (אַח, ʾakh) as the accusative sign (אֵת, ʾet), thereby giving the impression that Elhanan, not David, killed Goliath. Thus in all probability the original text read, “Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite killed the brother of Goliath.”

*Study note:* In this long song of thanks, David affirms that God is his faithful protector. He recalls in highly poetic fashion how God intervened in awesome power and delivered him from death. His experience demonstrates that God vindicates those who are blameless and remain loyal to him. True to his promises, God gives the king victory on the battlefield and enables him to subdue nations. A parallel version of the song appears in {{Psalm 18|Ps 18}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “spoke.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the day,” or “at the time.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and from the hand of Saul.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally “is my rock”; CEV “mighty rock”; TEV “is my protector.” This metaphor pictures God as a rocky, relatively inaccessible summit, where one would be able to find protection from enemies. See {{1 Samuel 23:25|1 Sam 23:25}}, {{1 Samuel 23:28|28}}.

*Translator's note:* Traditionally “my fortress”; TEV “my strong fortress”; NCV “my protection.”

*Study note:* *My stronghold*. David often found safety in such strongholds. See {{1 Samuel 22:4|1 Sam 22:4-5}}; {{1 Samuel 24:22|24:22}}; {{2 Samuel 5:9|2 Sam 5:9}}, {{2 Samuel 5:17|17}}; {{2 Samuel 23:14|23:14}}.

*Text-critical note:* The translation (along with many English versions, e.g., NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT) follows the LXX in reading אֱלֹהַי (ʾelohay, “my God”) rather than MT’s אֱלֹהֵי (ʾelohe, “the God of”). See {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “in whom.”

*Study note:* Though some see “horn” as referring to a horn-shaped peak of a hill, or to the “horns” of an altar where one could find refuge, it is more likely that the horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (see {{Deuteronomy 33:17|Deut 33:17}}; {{1 Kings 22:11|1 Kgs 22:11}}; {{Psalm 92:10|Ps 92:10}}). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt the horn” signifies military victory (see {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Sam 2:10}}; {{Psalm 89:17|Pss 89:17}}, {{Psalm 89:24|24}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}; Lam 2:17). In the ancient Near East powerful warrior-kings would sometimes compare themselves to a goring bull that uses its horns to kill its enemies. For examples, see P. Miller, “El the Warrior,” *HTR* 60 (1967): 422-25, and R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 135-36. {{2 Samuel 22:3|2 Sam 22:3}} uses the metaphor of the horn in a slightly different manner. Here the Lord himself is compared to a horn. He is to the psalmist what the horn is to the ox, a source of defense and victory.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the horn of my salvation,” or “my saving horn.”

*Translator's note:* The parallel version of the song in {{Psalm 18|Ps 18}} does not include this last line.

*Translator's note:* In this song of thanksgiving, where David recalls how the Lord delivered him, the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense (cf. CEV “I prayed”), not an imperfect (as in many English versions).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “worthy of praise, I cried out [to] the Lord.” Some take מְהֻלָּל (mehullal, “worthy of praise”) with what precedes and translate, “the praiseworthy one,” or “praiseworthy.” However, the various epithets in vv. {{2 Samuel 22:1|1-2}} have the first person pronominal suffix, unlike מְהֻלָּל. If one follows the traditional verse division and takes מְהֻלָּל with what follows, it is best understood as substantival and as appositional to יְהוָה (yehvah, “Yahweh”), resulting in “[to the] praiseworthy one I cried out, [to the] Lord.”

*Translator's note:* The noun נַחַל (nakhal) usually refers to a river or stream, but in this context the plural form likely refers to the currents of the sea (see vv. {{2 Samuel 22:15|15-16}}).

*Translator's note:* The noun בְלִיַּעַל (beliyyaʿal) is used here as an epithet for death. Elsewhere it is a common noun meaning “wickedness, uselessness” (see *HALOT* 133-34 s.v. בְּלִיַּעַל). It is often associated with rebellion against authority and other crimes that result in societal disorder and anarchy. The phrase “man/son of wickedness” refers to one who opposes God and the order he has established. The term becomes an appropriate title for death, which, through human forces, launches an attack against God’s chosen servant.

*Translator's note:* In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not an imperfect. (Note the perfect verbal form in the parallel/preceding line.) The verb בָּעַת (baʿat) sometimes by metonymy carries the nuance “frighten,” but the parallelism (note “engulfed” in the preceding line) favors the meaning “overwhelm” here.

*Translator's note:* “Sheol,” personified here as David’s enemy, is the underworld, place of the dead in primitive Hebrew cosmology.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “surrounded me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “confronted me.”

*Translator's note:* In this poetic narrative the two prefixed verbal forms in v. {{2 Samuel 22:7|7a}} are best understood as preterites indicating past tense, not imperfects. Note the use of the *vav* consecutive with the prefixed verbal form that follows in v. {{2 Samuel 22:7|7b}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from his temple.” Verse {{2 Samuel 22:10|10}}, which pictures God descending from the sky, indicates that the heavenly, not earthly, temple is in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my cry for help [entered] his ears.”

*Translator's note:* *The earth heaved and shook*. The imagery pictures an earthquake, in which the earth’s surface rises and falls. The earthquake motif is common in Old Testament theophanies of God as warrior and in ancient Near eastern literary descriptions of warring gods and kings. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 160-62.

*Translator's note:* {{Psalm 18:7|Psalm 18:7}} reads “the roots of the mountains.”

*Translator's note:* In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not an imperfect. Note the three prefixed verbal forms with *vav* consecutive in the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “within” or “[from] within.” For a discussion of the use of the preposition ב (bet) here, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 163-64.

*Translator's note:* Or “in his anger.” The noun אַף (ʾaf) can carry the abstract meaning “anger,” but the parallelism (note “from his mouth”) suggests the more concrete meaning “nose” here (most English versions, “nostrils”). See also v. {{2 Samuel 22:16|16}}, “the powerful breath of your nose.”

*Study note:* For other examples of *fire* as a weapon in Old Testament theophanies and ancient Near Eastern portrayals of warring gods and kings, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 165-67.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fire from his mouth devoured.” In this poetic narrative the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not an imperfect. Note the two perfect verbal forms in the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “coals burned from him.” Perhaps the psalmist pictures God’s fiery breath igniting coals (see {{Job 41:21|Job 41:21}}), which he then hurls as weapons (see {{Psalm 120:4|Ps 120:4}}).

*Translator's note:* The verb נָטָה (natah) can carry the sense “[to cause to] bend; [to cause to] bow down” (see *HALOT* 693 s.v. נָטָה). For example, {{Genesis 49:15|Gen 49:15}} pictures Issachar as a donkey that “bends” its shoulder or back under a burden (cf. KJV, NASB, NRSV “He bowed the heavens”; NAB “He inclined the heavens”). Here the Lord causes the sky, pictured as a dome or vault, to bend or sink down as he descends in the storm.

*Translator's note:* Or “rode upon.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a cherub” (so KJV, NAB, NRSV); NIV “the cherubim” (plural); TEV “his winged creature”; CEV “flying creatures.”

*Study note:* *A winged angel*. Cherubim, as depicted in the Old Testament, possess both human and animal (lion, ox, and eagle) characteristics (see {{Ezekiel 1:10|Ezek 1:10}}; {{Ezekiel 10:14|10:14}}, {{Ezekiel 10:21|21}}; {{Ezekiel 41:18|41:18}}). They are pictured as winged creatures ({{Exodus 25:20|Exod 25:20}}; {{Exodus 37:9|37:9}}; {{1 Kings 6:24|1 Kgs 6:24-27}}; {{Ezekiel 10:8|Ezek 10:8}}, {{Ezekiel 10:19|19}}) and serve as the very throne of God when the ark of the covenant is in view ({{Psalm 80:1|Pss 80:1}}; {{Psalm 99:1|99:1}}; see {{Numbers 7:89|Num 7:89}}; {{1 Samuel 4:4|1 Sam 4:4}}; {{2 Samuel 6:2|2 Sam 6:2}}; {{2 Kings 19:15|2 Kgs 19:15}}). The picture of the Lord seated on the cherubim suggests they might be used by him as a vehicle, a function they carry out in {{Ezekiel 1:22|Ezek 1:22-28}} (the “living creatures” mentioned here are identified as cherubim in {{Ezekiel 10:20|Ezek 10:20}}). In {{Psalm 18:10|Ps 18:10}} the image of a cherub serves to personify the wind (see the next line).

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows very many medieval Hebrew mss in reading וַיֵּדֶא (vayyedeʾ, “and he glided”; cf. NIV “soared”; NCV “raced”) rather than MT וַיֵּרָא (vayyeraʾ, “and he appeared,” so NASB, CEV). See as well the Syriac Peshitta, Targum, Vulgate, and the parallel version in {{Psalm 18:10|Ps 18:10}}, which preserves the original reading (see the note there).

*Study note:* *The wings of the wind*. Verse {{2 Samuel 22:10|10}} may depict the Lord mounting a cherub, which is in turn propelled by the wind current. Another option is that two different vehicles (a cherub and the wind) are envisioned. A third option is that the wind is personified as a cherub. For a discussion of ancient Near Eastern parallels to the imagery in v. {{2 Samuel 22:10|10}}, see M. Weinfeld, “‘Rider of the Clouds’ and ‘Gatherer of the Clouds’,” *JANESCU* 5 (1973): 422-24.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “he made darkness around him coverings.” The parallel text in {{Psalm 18:11|Ps 18:11}} reads “he made darkness his hiding place around him, his covering.” {{2 Samuel 22:12|2 Sam 22:12}} omits “his hiding place” and pluralizes “covering.” {{Psalm 18:11|Psalm 18:11}} may include a conflation of synonyms (“his hiding place” and “his covering”) or {{2 Samuel 22:12|2 Sam 22:12}} may be the result of haplography/homoioarcton. Note that three successive words in {{Psalm 18:11|Ps 18:11}} begin with the letter ס (samek): סִתְרוֹ סְבִיבוֹתָיו סֻכָּתוֹ (sitro sevivotayv sukkato).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “a sieve of water, clouds of clouds.” The form חַשְׁרַת (khashrat) is a construct of חַשְׁרָה (khashrah, “sieve”), which occurs only here in the OT. A cognate Ugaritic noun means “sieve,” and a related verb חשׁר (“to sift”) is attested in post-biblical Hebrew and Aramaic (see *HALOT* 363 s.v. *חשׁר). The phrase חַשְׁרַת־מַיִם (khashrat mayim) means literally “a sieve of water.” It pictures the rain clouds as a sieve through which the rain falls to the ground. (See F. M. Cross and D. N. Freedman, *Studies in Ancient Yahwistic Poetry*, 146, note 33.)

*Text-critical note:* The parallel text in {{Psalm 18:12|Ps 18:12}} reads “from the brightness in front of him his clouds came, hail and coals of fire.” The Lucianic family of texts within the Greek tradition of {{2 Samuel 22:13|2 Sam 22:13}} seems to assume the underlying Hebrew text: מִנֹּגַהּ נֶגְדּוֹ עָבְרוּ בָּרָד וְגַחֲלֵי אֵשׁ (minnogah negdo ʿaveru barad vegakhale ʾesh, “from the brightness in front of him came hail and coals of fire”) which is the basis for the present translation. The textual situation is perplexing and the identity of the original text uncertain. The verbs עָבְרוּ (ʿaveru; {{Psalm 18:12|Ps 18:12}}) and בָּעֲרוּ (baʿaru, {{2 Samuel 22:13|2 Sam 22:13}}) appear to be variants involving a transposition of the first two letters. The noun עָבָיו (ʿavayv, “his clouds”; {{Psalm 18:12|Ps 18:12}}) may be virtually dittographic (note the following עָבְרוּ), or it could have accidentally dropped from the text of {{2 Samuel 22:13|2 Sam 22:13}} by virtual haplography (note the preceding בָּעֲרוּ [baʿaru], which might have originally read עָבְרוּ). The term בָּרָד (barad, “hail”; {{Psalm 18:12|Ps 18:12}}) may be virtually dittographic (note the preceding עָבְרוּ), or it could have dropped from {{2 Samuel 22:13|2 Sam 22:13}} by virtual haplography (note the preceding בָּעֲרוּ, which might have originally read עָבְרוּ). For a fuller discussion of the text, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 74-76.

*Translator's note:* The shortened theme vowel indicates that the prefixed verbal form is a preterite.

*Study note:* This divine title (עֶלְיוֹן, ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially {{Psalm 47:2|Ps 47:2}}.

*Study note:* Thunder is a common motif in Old Testament theophanies and in ancient Near Eastern portrayals of the storm god and warring kings. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 179-83.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “offered his voice.” In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not an imperfect. Note the preterite form in the preceding line. The text of {{Psalm 18:13|Ps 18:13}} adds at this point, “hail and coals of fire.” These words are probably accidentally added from v. {{2 Samuel 22:12|12b}}; they do not appear in {{2 Samuel 22:14|2 Sam 22:14}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sent.”

*Translator's note:* The pronominal suffixes on the verbs “scattered” and “routed” (see the next line) refer to David’s enemies. Some argue that the suffixes refer to the arrows, in which case one might translate “shot them far and wide” and “made them move noisily,” respectively. They argue that the enemies have not been mentioned since v. {{2 Samuel 22:4|4}} and are not again mentioned until v. {{2 Samuel 22:17|17}}. However, usage of the verbs פוּץ (puts, “scatter”) and הָמַם (hamam, “rout”) elsewhere in Holy War accounts suggests the suffixes refer to enemies. Enemies are frequently pictured in such texts as scattered and/or routed (see {{Exodus 14:24|Exod 14:24}}; {{Exodus 23:27|23:27}}; {{Numbers 10:35|Num 10:35}}; {{Joshua 10:10|Josh 10:10}}; {{Judges 4:15|Judg 4:15}}; {{1 Samuel 7:10|1 Sam 7:10}}; {{1 Samuel 11:11|11:11}}; {{Psalm 68:1|Ps 68:1}}).

*Study note:* *Lightning* is a common motif in OT theophanies and in ancient Near Eastern portrayals of the storm god and warring kings. Arrows and lightning bolts are associated in other texts (see {{Psalm 77:17|Pss 77:17-18}}; {{Psalm 144:6|144:6}}; Zech 9:14), as well as in ancient Near Eastern art. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 187, 190-92.

*Translator's note:* Or “channels.”

*Translator's note:* Or “foundations.”

*Translator's note:* The noun is derived from the verb גָעַר (gaʿar) which is often understood to mean “rebuke.” In some cases it is apparent that scolding or threatening is in view (see {{Genesis 37:10|Gen 37:10}}; {{Ruth 2:16|Ruth 2:16}}; Zech 3:2). However, in militaristic contexts this translation is inadequate, for the verb refers in this setting to the warrior’s battle cry, which terrifies and paralyzes the enemy. See A. Caquot, *TDOT* 3:53, and note the use of the verb in {{Psalm 68:30|Pss 68:30}}; {{Psalm 106:9|106:9}}; and Nah 1:4, as well as the related noun in {{Job 26:11|Job 26:11}}; {{Psalm 9:5|Pss 9:5}}; {{Psalm 76:6|76:6}}; {{Psalm 104:7|104:7}}; {{Isaiah 50:2|Isa 50:2}}; {{Isaiah 51:20|51:20}}; {{Isaiah 66:15|66:15}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blast of the breath” (literally, “breath of breath”) employs an appositional genitive. Synonyms are joined in a construct relationship to emphasize the single idea. For a detailed discussion of the grammatical point with numerous examples, see Y. Avishur, “Pairs of Synonymous Words in the Construct State (and in Appositional Hendiadys) in Biblical Hebrew,” *Semitics* 2 (1971): 17-81.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stretched.” Perhaps “his hand” should be supplied by ellipsis (see {{Psalm 144:7|Ps 144:7}}). In this poetic narrative context the three prefixed verbal forms in this verse are best understood as preterites indicating past tense, not imperfects.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mighty waters.” The waters of the sea symbolize the psalmist’s powerful enemies, as well as the realm of death they represent (see v. {{2 Samuel 22:5|5}} and {{Psalm 144:7|Ps 144:7}}).
*Translator's note:* The singular refers either to personified death or collectively to the psalmist’s enemies. The following line, which refers to “those [plural] who hate me,” favors the latter.

*Translator's note:* The same verb is translated “trapped” in v. {{2 Samuel 22:6|6}}. In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not imperfect. Cf. NAB, NCV, TEV, NLT “attacked.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “became my support.”
*Translator's note:* Or “delighted in me” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not imperfect.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to my righteousness.” As vv. {{2 Samuel 22:22|22-25}} make clear, David refers here to his unwavering obedience to God’s commands. He explains that the Lord was pleased with him and willing to deliver him because he had been loyal to God and obedient to his commandments. Ancient Near Eastern literature contains numerous parallels. A superior (a god or king) would typically reward a subject (a king or the servant of a king, respectively) for loyalty and obedience. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 211-13.

*Translator's note:* The unreduced Hiphil prefixed verbal form appears to be an imperfect, in which case the psalmist would be generalizing. However, both the preceding and following contexts (see especially v. {{2 Samuel 22:25|25}}) suggest he is narrating his experience. Despite its unreduced form, the verb is better taken as a preterite. For other examples of unreduced Hiphil preterites, see {{Psalm 55:14|Pss 55:14a}}; {{Psalm 68:9|68:9a}}, {{Psalm 68:10|10b}}; {{Psalm 80:8|80:8a}}; {{Psalm 89:43|89:43a}}; {{Psalm 107:38|107:38b}}; {{Psalm 116:6|116:6b}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to the purity of my hands he repaid to me.” Hands suggest activity and behavior.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for I have kept the ways of the Lord.” The phrase “ways of the Lord” refers here to the “conduct required” by the Lord (see *HALOT* 232 s.v. דֶרֶךְ). In {{Psalm 25|Ps 25}} the Lord’s “ways” are associated with his covenantal demands (see vv. {{2 Samuel 22:4|4}}, {{2 Samuel 22:9|9-10}}). See also {{Psalm 119:3|Ps 119:3}} (cf. vv. {{2 Samuel 22:1|1}}, {{2 Samuel 22:4|4}}), as well as {{Deuteronomy 8:6|Deut 8:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 10:12|10:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 11:22|11:22}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:9|19:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:17|26:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:9|28:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:16|30:16}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I have not acted wickedly from my God.” The statement is elliptical, the idea being, “I have not acted wickedly and, in so doing, departed from my God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for all his regulations are before me.” The term מִשְׁפָּטָו (mishpatav, “his regulations”) refers to God’s covenantal requirements, especially those which the king is responsible to follow (cf {{Deuteronomy 17:18|Deut 17:18-20}}). See also {{Psalm 19:9|Pss 19:9}} (cf vv. {{2 Samuel 22:7|7-8}}); {{Psalm 89:30|89:30}}; {{Psalm 147:20|147:20}} (cf v. {{2 Samuel 22:19|19}}), as well as the numerous uses of the term in {{Psalm 119|Ps 119}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his rules, I do not turn aside from it.” {{Psalm 18:22|Ps 18:22}} reads, “and his rules I do not turn aside from me.” The prefixed verbal form is probably an imperfect; David here generalizes about his loyalty to God’s commands. The Lord’s “rules” are the stipulations of the covenant which the king was responsible to obey (see {{Psalm 89:31|Ps 89:31}}; cf v. {{2 Samuel 22:30|30}} and {{Deuteronomy 17:18|Deut 17:18-20}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from my sin,” that is, from making it my own in any way. Leading a “blameless” life meant that the king would be loyal to God’s covenant, purge the government and society of evil and unjust officials, and reward loyalty to the Lord (see {{Psalm 101|Ps 101}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to my righteousness.” See v. {{2 Samuel 22:21|21}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to my purity before his eyes.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal forms in vv. {{2 Samuel 22:26|26-30}} draw attention to God’s characteristic actions. Based on his experience, the psalmist generalizes about God’s just dealings with people (vv. {{2 Samuel 22:26|26-28}}) and about the way in which God typically empowers him on the battlefield (vv. {{2 Samuel 22:29|29-30}}). The Hitpael stem is used in vv. {{2 Samuel 22:26|26-27}} in a reflexive resultative (or causative) sense. God makes himself loyal, etc. in the sense that he conducts or reveals himself as such. On this use of the Hitpael stem, see GKC 149-50 §54.*e*.

*Translator's note:* Or “to a faithful follower.” A חָסִיד (khasid, “faithful follower”) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see {{Psalm 4:3|Pss 4:3}}; {{Psalm 12:1|12:1}}; {{Psalm 16:10|16:10}}; {{Psalm 31:23|31:23}}; {{Psalm 37:28|37:28}}; {{Psalm 86:2|86:2}}; {{Psalm 97:10|97:10}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “innocent.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “a warrior of innocence.” The parallel text in {{Psalm 18:25|Ps 18:25}} reads, probably correctly, גֶּבֶר (gever, “man”) instead of גִּבּוֹר (gibbor, “warrior”).

*Translator's note:* Or “blameless.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows two medieval Hebrew mss in reading תִּתְפַּתָּל (titpattal) from the root פָּתַל (patal, “to twist”), rather than the MT תִּתַּפָּל (tittappal, from the root תָּפַל (tafal, “to be tasteless,” “behave silly”; cf. KJV “unsavoury”). See as well the parallel passage in {{Psalm 18:26|Ps 18:26}}. The verb פָּתַל (patal) is used in only three other texts. In {{Genesis 30:8|Gen 30:8}} it means literally “to wrestle,” or “to twist.” In {{Job 5:13|Job 5:13}} it refers to devious individuals, and in {{Proverbs 8:8|Prov 8:8}} to deceptive words. Cf. NAB, NASB “astute”; NIV “shrewd”; NRSV “perverse”; TEV, NLT “hostile.”

*Translator's note:* The adjective עִקֵּשׁ (ʿiqqesh) has the basic nuance “twisted; crooked,” and by extension refers to someone or something that is morally perverse. It appears frequently in Proverbs, where it is used of evil people ({{Proverbs 22:5|22:5}}), speech ({{Proverbs 8:8|8:8}}; {{Proverbs 19:1|19:1}}), thoughts ({{Proverbs 11:20|11:20}}; {{Proverbs 17:20|17:20}}) and life styles ({{Proverbs 2:15|2:15}}; {{Proverbs 28:6|28:6}}). A righteous king opposes such people ({{Psalm 101:4|Ps 101:4}}). Verses {{2 Samuel 22:26|26-27}} affirm God’s justice. He responds to people in accordance with their moral character. His response mirrors their actions. The faithful and blameless find God to be loyal and reliable in his dealings with them. But deceivers discover he is able and willing to use deceit to destroy them. For a more extensive discussion of the theme of divine deception in the OT, see R. B. Chisholm, “Does God Deceive?” *BSac* 155 (1998): 11-28.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “humble” (so NIV, NRSV, NLT; note the contrast with those who are proud).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “but your eyes are upon the proud, you bring low.” {{Psalm 18:27|Psalm 18:27}} reads “but proud eyes you bring low.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.” The translation assumes that כִּי (ki) is asseverative here.

*Text-critical note:* Many medieval Hebrew mss, some LXX mss, and the Syriac Peshitta support reading תָּאִיר (taʾir, “you cause to shine”) before the words “my lamp.” See {{Psalm 18:28|Ps 18:28}}. The metaphor, which likens the Lord to a lamp or light, pictures him as the psalmist’s source of life. For other examples of “lamp” used in this way, see {{Job 18:6|Job 18:6}}; {{Job 21:17|21:17}}; {{Proverbs 13:9|Prov 13:9}}; {{Proverbs 20:20|20:20}}; {{Proverbs 24:20|24:20}}. For other examples of “light” as a symbol for life, see {{Job 3:20|Job 3:20}}; {{Job 33:30|33:30}}; {{Psalm 56:13|Ps 56:13}}.

*Text-critical note:* The Lucianic Greek recension and Vulgate understand this verb to be second person rather than third person as in the MT. But this is probably the result of reading the preceding word “Lord” as a vocative under the influence of the vocative in the first part of the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my darkness.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.” The translation assumes that כִּי (ki) is asseverative here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will run.” The imperfect verbal forms in v. {{2 Samuel 22:30|30}} indicate the subject’s potential or capacity to perform an action. Though one might expect a preposition to follow the verb here, this need not be the case with the verb רוּץ (ruts; see {{1 Samuel 17:22|1 Sam 17:22}}). Some emend the Qal to a Hiphil form of the verb and translate, “I put to flight [literally, “cause to run”] an army.”

*Translator's note:* More specifically, the noun refers to a raiding party or to a contingent of troops (see *HALOT* 177 s.v. II גְדוּד). The picture of a divinely empowered warrior charging against an army in almost superhuman fashion appears elsewhere in ancient Near Eastern literature. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 228.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by my God.”

*Translator's note:* David uses hyperbole to emphasize his God-given military superiority.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[As for] the God, his way is blameless.” The term הָאֵל (haʾel, “the God”) stands as a nominative (or genitive) absolute in apposition to the resumptive pronominal suffix on “way.” The prefixed article emphasizes his distinctiveness as the one true God (see BDB 42 s.v. II אֵל 6; {{Deuteronomy 33:26|Deut 33:26}}). God’s “way” in this context refers to his protective and salvific acts in fulfillment of his promise (see also {{Deuteronomy 32:4|Deut 32:4}}; {{Psalm 67:2|Pss 67:2}}; {{Psalm 77:13|77:13}} [note vv. {{Psalm 77:11|11-12}}, {{Psalm 77:14|14}}]; {{Psalm 103:7|103:7}}; {{Psalm 138:5|138:5}}; {{Psalm 145:17|145:17}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the word of the Lord is purified.” The Lord’s “word” probably refers here to his oracle(s) of victory delivered to the psalmist before the battle(s) described in the following context. See also {{Psalm 12:5|Pss 12:5-7}} and {{Psalm 138:2|138:2-3}}. David frequently received such oracles before going into battle (see {{1 Samuel 23:2|1 Sam 23:2}}, {{1 Samuel 23:4|4-5}}, {{1 Samuel 23:10|10-12}}; {{1 Samuel 30:8|30:8}}; {{2 Samuel 5:19|2 Sam 5:19}}). The Lord’s word of promise is absolutely reliable; it is compared to metal that has been refined in fire and cleansed of impurities. See {{Psalm 12:6|Ps 12:6}}. In the ancient Near East kings would typically seek and receive oracles from their god(s) prior to battle. For examples, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 241-42.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.” The translation assumes that כִּי (ki) is asseverative here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor of protection.

*Translator's note:* The rhetorical questions anticipate the answer, “No one.” In this way the psalmist indicates that the Lord is the only true God and reliable source of protection. See also {{Deuteronomy 32:39|Deut 32:39}}, where the Lord affirms that he is the only true God. Note as well the emphasis on his role as protector (צוּר, tsur, “rocky cliff”) in {{Deuteronomy 32:4|Deut 32:4}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:15|15}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:17|17-18}}, {{Deuteronomy 32:30|30}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God.” See the note at v. {{2 Samuel 22:31|31}}.

*Text-critical note:* 4QSama has מְאַזְּרֵנִי (meʾazzereni, “the one girding me with strength”) rather than the MT מָעוּזִּי (maʿuzzi, “my refuge”). See as well {{Psalm 18:32|Ps 18:32}}.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form with vav consecutive here carries along the generalizing tone of the preceding line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he sets free (from the verb נָתַר, natar) [the] blameless, his [*Kethib*; “my” (*Qere*)] way.” The translation follows {{Psalm 18:32|Ps 18:32}} in reading “he made my path smooth.” The term תָּמִים (tamim, “smooth”) usually carries a moral or ethical connotation, “blameless, innocent.” However, in {{Psalm 18:33|Ps 18:33}} it refers to a pathway free of obstacles. The reality underlying the metaphor is the psalmist’s ability to charge into battle without tripping (see vv. {{2 Samuel 22:33|33}}, {{2 Samuel 22:36|36}}).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “[the one who] makes his feet like [those of] a deer.” The translation follows the *Qere* and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading רַגְלַי (raglay, “my feet”) rather than the MT רַגְלָיו (raglayv, “his feet”). See as well {{Psalm 18:33|Ps 18:33}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and on my high places he makes me walk.” The imperfect verbal form emphasizes God’s characteristic provision. The psalmist compares his agility in battle to the ability of a deer to negotiate rugged, high terrain without falling or being injured. Habakkuk uses similar language to describe his faith during difficult times. See {{Habakkuk 3:19|Hab 3:19}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “teaches.”

*Translator's note:* The psalmist attributes his skill with weapons to divine enabling. Egyptian reliefs picture gods teaching the king how to shoot a bow. See O. Keel, *Symbolism of the Biblical World*, 265.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a bow of bronze is bent by my arms.” The verb נָחֵת (nakhet) apparently means “to pull back; to bend” here (see *HALOT* 692 s.v. נחת). The bronze bow referred to here was probably laminated with bronze strips, or a purely ceremonial or decorative bow made entirely from bronze. In the latter case the language is hyperbolic, for such a weapon would not be functional in battle.

*Translator's note:* Another option is to translate the prefixed verb with vav consecutive with a past tense, “you gave me.” Several prefixed verbal forms with vav consecutive also appear in vv. {{2 Samuel 22:38|38-44}}. The present translation understands this section as a description of what generally happened when the author charged into battle, but another option is to understand the section as narrative and translate accordingly.

*Text-critical note:* {{Psalm 18:35|Psalm 18:35}} contains an additional line following this one, which reads “your right hand supports me.” It may be omitted here due to homoioarcton. See the note at {{Psalm 18:35|Ps 18:35}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you give me the shield of your deliverance”; KJV, ASV “the shield of thy (your NRSV, NLT) salvation”; NIV84 “your shield of victory”; NIV11 “your saving help my shield.” Ancient Near Eastern literature often refers to a god giving a king special weapons. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 260-61.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your answer makes me great.” David refers to God’s willingness to answer his prayer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “step.” “Step” probably refers metonymically to the path upon which the psalmist walks. Another option is to translate, “you widen my stride.” This would suggest that God gives him the capacity to run quickly.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lower legs.” On the meaning of the Hebrew noun, which occurs only here, see H. R. Cohen, *Biblical Hapax Legomena* (SBLDS), 112. A cognate Akkadian noun means “lower leg.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you clothed me with strength for battle.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you make those who rise against me kneel beneath me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [as for] my enemies, you give to me [the] back [or “neck” ].” The idiom “give [the] back” means “to cause [one] to turn the back and run away.” See {{Exodus 23:27|Exod 23:27}} and *HALOT* 888 s.v. II ערף.

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows one medieval Hebrew ms and the ancient versions in reading the Piel יְשַׁוְּעוּ (yeshavveʿu, “they cry for help”) rather than the Qal of the MT יִשְׁעוּ (yishʿu, “they look about for help”). See {{Psalm 18:41|Ps 18:41}} as well.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but there is no deliverer.”

*Translator's note:* The words “they cry out” are not in the Hebrew text. This reference to the psalmists’ enemies crying out for help to the Lord suggests that the psalmist refers here to enemies within the covenant community, rather than foreigners. However, the militaristic context suggests foreign enemies are in view. Ancient Near Eastern literature indicates that defeated enemies would sometimes cry out for mercy to the god(s) of their conqueror. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 271.
*Translator's note:* Or “mud” (so NAB, NIV, CEV). See *HALOT* 374 s.v. טִיט.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the strivings of my people.” In this context רִיב (riv, “striving”) probably has a militaristic sense (as in {{Judges 12:2|Judg 12:2}}; {{Isaiah 41:11|Isa 41:11}}), and עַם (ʿam, “people”) probably refers more specifically to an army (for other examples, see the verses listed in BDB 766 s.v. עַם 2.d). The suffix “my” suggests David is referring to attacks by his own countrymen, the “people” being Israel. However, the parallel text in {{Psalm 18:43|Ps 18:43}} omits the suffix.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a people whom I did not know serve me.” In this context the verb “know” (יָדַע, yadaʿ) probably refers to formal recognition by treaty. People who were once not under the psalmist’s authority now willingly submit to his rulership to avoid being conquered militarily (see vv. {{2 Samuel 22:45|45-46}}). The language may recall the events recorded in {{2 Samuel 8:9|2 Sam 8:9-10}} and {{2 Samuel 10:19|10:19}}.

*Translator's note:* For the meaning “to be weak; to be powerless” for the verb כָּחַשׁ (kakhash), see {{Psalm 109:24|Ps 109:24}}. Verse {{2 Samuel 22:46|46}}, which also mentions foreigners, favors this interpretation. Another option is to translate “cower in fear” (see {{Deuteronomy 33:29|Deut 33:29}}; {{Psalm 66:3|Pss 66:3}}; {{Psalm 81:15|81:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at a report of an ear they submit to me.” The report of David’s exploits is so impressive that those who hear it submit to his rulership without putting up a fight.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wither, wear out.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation assumes a reading וְיַחְרְגוּ (veyakhregu, “and they quaked”) rather than the MT וְיַחְגְּרוּ (veyakhgeru, “and they girded themselves”). See the note at {{Psalm 18:45|Ps 18:45}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “prisons.” Their besieged cities are compared to prisons.

*Translator's note:* Elsewhere the construction חַי־יְהוָה (khay yehvah) is used exclusively as an oath formula, but this is not the case here, for no oath follows. Here the statement is an affirmation of the Lord’s active presence and intervention. In contrast to pagan deities, he demonstrates that he is the living God by rescuing and empowering the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor for protection.

*Translator's note:* Or “blessed [i.e., praised] be.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God of the rock of my deliverance.” The term צוּר (tsur, “rock”) is probably accidentally repeated from the previous line. The parallel version in {{Psalm 18:46|Ps 18:46}} has simply “the God of my deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* The words “as king” are supplied in the translation for clarification. In the Psalms the verb רוּם (rum, “be exalted”) when used of God, refers to his exalted position as king ({{Psalm 99:2|Pss 99:2}}; {{Psalm 113:4|113:4}}; {{Psalm 138:6|138:6}}) and/or his self-revelation as king through his mighty deeds of deliverance ({{Psalm 21:13|Pss 21:13}}; {{Psalm 46:10|46:10}}; {{Psalm 57:5|57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:11|11}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The God is the one who grants vengeance to me.” The plural form of the noun “vengeance” indicates degree here, suggesting complete vengeance or vindication. In the ancient Near East military victory was sometimes viewed as a sign that one’s God had judged in favor of the victor, avenging and/or vindicating him. See, for example, {{Judges 11:27|Judg 11:27}}, {{Judges 11:32|32-33}}, {{Judges 11:36|36}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [is the one who] brings down nations beneath me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [the one who] brings me out from my enemies.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you lift me up.” In light of the preceding and following references to deliverance, the verb רוּם (rum) probably here refers to being rescued from danger (see {{Psalm 9:13|Ps 9:13}}). However, it could mean “exalt; elevate” here, indicating that the Lord has given him victory over his enemies and forced them to acknowledge the psalmist’s superiority.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from those who rise against me.”

*Study note:* This probably alludes to the fact that David will praise the Lord in the presence of the defeated *nations* when they, as his subjects, bring their tribute payments. Ideally God’s chosen king was to testify to the nations of God’s greatness. See J. Eaton, *Kingship and the Psalms* (SBT), 182-85.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to your name.” God’s “name” refers metonymically to his divine characteristics as suggested by his name, in this case “Lord,” the primary name of Israel’s covenant God which suggests his active presence with his people (see {{Exodus 3:12|Exod 3:12-15}}).

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Kethib* and the ancient versions in reading מַגְדִּיל (magdil, “he magnifies”) rather than the *Qere* and many medieval Hebrew mss of the MT which read מִגְדּוֹל (migdol, “tower”). See {{Psalm 18:50|Ps 18:50}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the one who] does loyalty to his anointed one.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the anointed one of the God of Jacob.”

*Translator's note:* Or “pleasant.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rock,” used as a metaphor of divine protection.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “For not thus [is] my house with God?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for all my deliverance and every desire, surely does he not make [it] grow?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and with fire they are completely burned up in [the place where they] remain.” The infinitive absolute is used before the finite verb to emphasize that they are completely consumed by the fire.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word is sometimes rendered as “the three,” but BDB is probably correct in taking it to refer to military officers (BDB 1026 s.v. שְׁלִישִׁי). In that case the etymological connection of this word to the Hebrew numerical adjective for “three” can be explained as originating with a designation for the *third* warrior in a chariot.

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows some LXX mss (see 1 Chr 11:11 as well) in reading הוּא עוֹרֵר אֶת־חֲנִיתוֹ (huʾ ʿorer ʾet khanito, “he raised up his spear”) rather than the MT’s הוּא עֲדִינוֹ הָעֶצְנִי (huʾ ʿadino haʿetsni [*Kethib* = הָעֶצְנוֹ, haʿetsno]; “Adino the Ezenite”). The emended text reads literally “he was wielding his spear against eight hundred, [who were] slain at one time.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “after him.”

*Text-critical note:* This follows the *Qere* and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading דֹּדוֹ (dodo) rather than the *Kethib* of the MT דֹּדַי (doday; cf. ASV, NIV, NLT). But see 1 Chr 27:4.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “went up.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “after him.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text is difficult here. The MT reads לַחַיָּה (lachayyah), which implies a rare use of the word חַיָּה (chayyah). The word normally refers to an animal, but if the MT is accepted it would here have the sense of a troop or community of people. BDB 312 s.v. II. חַיָּה, for example, understands the similar reference in v. {{2 Samuel 23:13|13}} to be to “a group of allied families, making a raid together.” But this works better in v. {{2 Samuel 23:13|13}} than it does in v. {{2 Samuel 23:11|11}}, where the context seems to suggest a particular staging location for a military operation. (See 1 Chr 11:15.) It therefore seems best to understand the word in v. {{2 Samuel 23:11|11}} as a place name with ה (he) directive. In that case the Masoretes mistook the word for the common term for an animal and then tried to make sense of it in this context.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of Hebrew אֶל־קָצִיר (ʾel qatsir) seems here to be “at the time of harvest,” although this is an unusual use of the phrase. As S. R. Driver points out, this preposition does not normally have the temporal sense of “in” or “during” (S. R. Driver, *Notes on the Hebrew Text and the Topography of the Books of Samuel*, 366).

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading שְׁלֹשָׁה (sheloshah, “three”) rather than the *Kethib* of the MT שְׁלֹשִׁים (sheloshim, “thirty”). “Thirty” is due to dittography of the following word and makes no sense in the context.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “went down…and approached.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Far be it to me, O Lord, from doing this.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Is it not] the blood of the men who were going with their lives?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “These things the three warriors did.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere*, many medieval Hebrew mss, the LXX, and Vulgate in reading הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה (hashelosha, “the three”) rather than the *Kethib* of the MT הַשָּׁלִשִׁי (hashalishi, “the third,” or “adjutant”). Two medieval Hebrew mss and the Syriac Peshitta have “thirty.”

*Study note:* The parallel text in 1 Chr 21:1 says, “An adversary opposed Israel, inciting David to count how many warriors Israel had.” The Samuel version gives an underlying theological perspective, while the Chronicler simply describes what happened from a human perspective. The adversary in 1 Chr 21:1 is likely a human enemy, probably a nearby nation whose hostility against Israel pressured David into numbering the people so he could assess his military strength. *Study note:* *Threshing sledges* were heavy boards used in ancient times for loosening grain from husks. On the bottom sides of these boards sharp stones were embedded, and the boards were then dragged across the grain on a threshing floor by an ox or donkey.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the equipment of the oxen.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text is difficult here. The translation reads עֶבֶד אֲדֹנִי (ʿeved ʾadoni, “the servant of my lord”) rather than the MT’s אֲרַוְנָה (ʾAravnah). In normal court etiquette a subject would not use his own name in this way, but would more likely refer to himself in the third person. The MT probably first sustained loss of עֶבֶד (ʿeved, “servant”), leading to confusion of the word for “my lord” with the name of the Jebusite referred to here.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “50 shekels of silver.” This would have been about 20 ounces (568 grams) of silver by weight.
